title: Notes from E-Marking Centre on SSC-I Physics Annual Examinations 2025
subject: Physics
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Part I Physics examination. It contains comments on candidates' responses to the 2025 SSC Part I Examination, indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: Candidates performed comparatively well in questions related to significant figures, Earth and space, and evaporation. Areas requiring improvement include questions based on stability, the process of heat transfer, motion due to gravity, momentum, power, and pressure in liquids.

questions.questionText:
i. How many significant figures are there in 0.0102030?
ii. List the rules of significant figures applied on the number given part (i).
questions.sloText: Apply the rules for rounding a number to the given number of significant figures to solve problems.
checkingHints: 1 mark for writing the correct number of significant figures (6 significant figures)
1 mark for writing any ONE rule of significant figures
questions.overallPerformance: Many candidates demonstrated a clear understanding of key concepts, such as the significance of trailing zeros in decimals and the exclusion of placeholder zeros before the first non-zero digit.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly identified 6 significant figures in the given number and mentioned any ONE of the rules of significant figures: counting non-zero digits, recognising significant middle and trailing zeros, and excluding non-significant leading zeros.
questions.weakerResponses: Weak responses presented answers in a disorganised table format with irrelevant terms or suggested 'three significant figures' without proper justification, either omitting the trailing zero (resulting in 5) or mistakenly including leading zeros.
suggestions: Focus on three key cases: leading zeros (never count), captive zeros (always count), and trailing zeros in decimals (always count).
Use worked examples like 0.001 (1 sig fig), 202 (3 sig figs), and 3.00 (3 sig figs) to demonstrate rules consistently.
questions.currentSloDescription: identify sources of errors (systematic and random) in the measurement;
questions.modelAnswer:
**(i) Identification of Measuring Instrument (1 Mark):**
• **Vernier Callipers** (used to measure internal/external diameter and depth up to $0.1\text{ mm}$ or $0.01\text{ cm}$).

**(ii) Least Count of Vernier Callipers (1 Mark):**
$$\text{Least Count (L.C.)} = \frac{\text{Smallest reading on main scale}}{\text{Total number of divisions on Vernier scale}} = 0.1\text{ mm} = 0.01\text{ cm}$$

questions.questionText: Describe the THREE states of equilibrium on the basis of the centre of gravity.
questions.sloText: Explain the effects of the position of the centre of gravity on the stability of simple objects.
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing each state of equilibrium (3 required). Note: No mark will be awarded for mentioning the name only.
questions.overallPerformance: A few candidates correctly defined all three states and effectively used the concept of centre of gravity (CoG) against each case. Overall performance required improvement in attention to detail.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses correctly named stable, unstable, and neutral equilibrium and linked each to the centre of gravity: stable as returning to the original position (CoG rises then falls), unstable as toppling (CoG lowers), and neutral as maintaining CoG height.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses listed vague statements such as 'It is vertically downwards' and 'The change in position of a body', which do not define stable, unstable, or neutral equilibrium.
suggestions: Connect each equilibrium state to the behaviour of the centre of gravity when objects are displaced (e.g., a book for stable equilibrium, a pencil for unstable).
Use diagrams showing how the height of the centre of gravity affects stability and restoring torque.
questions.currentSloDescription: explain different conditions of equilibrium with examples;
questions.modelAnswer:
**Effect of Lowering Centre of Gravity on Stability (3 Marks):**
1. **Condition for Stability:** An object's stability increases when its **centre of gravity ($G$)** is kept as low as possible and its **base area** is made as wide as possible.
2. **Reason:** Lowering the centre of gravity increases the tilt angle required before the vertical line of action of weight ($W = mg$) falls outside the base of support.
3. **Application:** Racing cars and double-decker buses are designed with heavy chassis/engines at the bottom and wide wheelbases so that the restoring moment returns them to stable equilibrium without toppling.

questions.questionText: The orbits of comets are large and elliptical as compared to the orbits of planets which are smaller and circular. Describe the difference in the shapes of orbits with the help of TWO reasons.
questions.sloText: Explain that the orbit of a comet differs from that of a planet.
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing each reason (Any 2 required)
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates struggled to accurately describe the difference between cometary elliptical orbits and planetary circular orbits. Some responses correctly mentioned gravitational influence and distance from the Sun.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses identified the highly eccentric elliptical paths of comets versus nearly circular planetary orbits and linked orbital shape to varying solar distance and gravitational pull.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses attributed orbit size solely to distance from the Sun while overlooking orbital velocity and angular momentum, or inaccurately linked magnetic fields to orbit shape.
suggestions: Use precise scientific terms (e.g., 'eccentric' for elliptical orbits) and clarify the role of gravitational forces.
Emphasise how gravitational pull decreases with distance (inverse-square law) and how elliptical orbits result from velocity and position conditions.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Given Data:**
• Mass of first car ($m_1$) = $1000\text{ kg}$
• Mass of second car ($m_2$) = $1000\text{ kg}$
• Distance between centres ($d$) = $2\text{ m}$
• Universal gravitational constant ($G$) = $6.673 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$

**Formula:**
$$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{d^2}$$

**Substitution & Calculation:**
$$F = \frac{(6.673 \times 10^{-11}) \times 1000 \times 1000}{(2)^2} = \frac{6.673 \times 10^{-5}}{4}$$
$$F = 1.67 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$$

questions.questionText: Write any THREE differences between evaporation and boiling.
checkingHints: 1 mark for EACH difference (Any 3 required)
questions.overallPerformance: Some candidates accurately distinguished evaporation and boiling, highlighting temperature requirements, bubble formation, and energy sources.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses highlighted three key scientific differences: (1) temperature requirement (boiling occurs at fixed boiling point while evaporation occurs at all temperatures), (2) bubble formation (absent in evaporation, present in boiling), and (3) surface vs. bulk phenomenon.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses wrote vague statements like 'State change' vs 'State does not change' or confused states of matter (claiming boiling converts solid into liquid).
suggestions: Use real-life examples (drying clothes vs. boiling water) to illustrate temperature dependence, bubble formation, and surface vs. bulk processes.
Present differences in a parallel comparison table.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Dependence of Liquid Pressure on Depth (3 Marks):**
1. **Hydrostatic Pressure Formula:** The pressure exerted by a liquid column at depth $h$ is given by:
$$P = \rho g h$$
where $\rho$ is the density of the liquid, $g$ is acceleration due to gravity, and $h$ is depth below the free surface.
2. **Direct Proportionality ($P \propto h$):** Since $\rho$ and $g$ are constant for a given liquid, hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth ($P \propto h$).
3. **Consequence:** Water emerges with the greatest horizontal speed and range from the lowest hole of a container (and dam walls are built thickest at the bottom) to withstand the maximum pressure at the greatest depth.

questions.questionText: A copper rod is 20 m long with a cross-sectional area of 4 m². If its two ends are kept at temperatures 200°C and 300°C respectively, calculate the amount of heat flowing across the rod in one second. (Note: Take the co-efficient of thermal conductivity as 386.4 J/m.K.s.)
questions.sloText: Solve word problems based on the thermal conductivity of solid conductors.
checkingHints: 1 mark for using the correct formula: Q/t = kA(T₁ - T₂)/L
1 mark for the correct substitution: (386.4 × 4 × 100) / 20
1 mark for writing the correct answer with SI unit: 7728 J (or J/s)
questions.overallPerformance: A few candidates demonstrated strong problem-solving skills and accurately applied the heat conduction formula with correct substitutions.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses applied Q/t = kAΔT / L and arrived at 7728 J with clear, logical steps and unit consistency.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses used invented formulas (such as ΔQ = m²t²/J) and mishandled units.
suggestions: Highlight each variable's physical meaning in Q/t = kAΔT/L (k = thermal conductivity, A = cross-sectional area, ΔT = temperature difference, L = length).
questions.currentSloDescription: explain the thermal expansion of liquids as the: a. real expansion, b. apparent expansion;
questions.modelAnswer:
**Given Data:**
• Mass of water ($m$) = $2\text{ kg}$
• Initial temperature ($T_1$) = $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$
• Final temperature ($T_2$) = $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$
• Change in temperature ($\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$) = $100 - 20 = 80\ ^\circ\text{C} = 80\text{ K}$
• Specific heat capacity of water ($c$) = $4200\text{ J}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}$

**Formula:**
$$\Delta Q = m c \Delta T$$

**Calculation:**
$$\Delta Q = 2\text{ kg} \times 4200\text{ J}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{K}^{-1} \times 80\text{ K} = 672,000\text{ J} = 6.72 \times 10^5\text{ J}\text{ (or }672\text{ kJ)}$$

questions.questionText: Zohan dropped a ball from a certain height. Its final velocity becomes 25 m/s when it reaches the ground. Now from the same height, if he throws the ball vertically downward with an initial velocity of 25 m/s, then calculate its final velocity. (Note: Take the value of acceleration due to gravity as 9.8 m/s².)
questions.sloText: Solve word problems related to freely falling bodies.
checkingHints: 1 mark for extracting the correct data
1 mark for writing the correct formula (2gh = vf² - vi²)
1 mark for substituting values for the dropped ball (vi = 0, vf = 25 m/s)
1 mark for finding the height h = 31.89 m
1 mark for substituting values for the thrown ball (vi = 25 m/s, h = 31.89 m)
1 mark for calculating the final velocity vf = 35.35 m/s
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates attempted part B, while those who attempted part A showed a wide range in applying two-stage kinematic equations.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses applied 2gh = vf² - vi² first with vi = 0 m/s to find height (31.89 m) and then with vi = 25 m/s to find the new final velocity (35.35 m/s).
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses added velocity and acceleration directly (25 + 9.8) or multiplied them to get 245 m/s, violating dimensional analysis.
suggestions: Use labelled diagrams to separate Stage 1 (dropped from rest) and Stage 2 (thrown downward from the same height).
Reinforce dimensional analysis so students never add velocity (m/s) and acceleration (m/s²).
questions.modelAnswer: Better responses applied 2gh = vf² - vi² first with vi = 0 m/s to find height (31.89 m) and then with vi = 25 m/s to find the new final velocity (35.35 m/s).

questions.questionText: State and explain Newton's 2nd law of motion and prove that the rate of change of momentum is equal to force.
questions.sloText: Explain the relationship between force and momentum.
checkingHints: 1 mark for each logical/mathematical step from F = ma and momentum P = mv to F = (Pf - Pi)/t = ΔP/Δt (6 marks total)
questions.overallPerformance: The majority of candidates attempted this part, with strong responses maintaining clear notation and step-by-step derivation.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses stated F = ma, defined initial momentum Pi = mvi and final momentum Pf = mvf, wrote ΔP = m(vf - vi), and divided by time t to prove F = ΔP/t.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses misstated momentum as 'the force used to make an object move' and wrote invalid equations without derivation.
suggestions: Emphasise F = ma and P = mv distinctly, then practice the algebraic substitution a = (vf - vi)/t into F = ma to yield F = ΔP/Δt.
questions.modelAnswer: Better responses stated F = ma, defined initial momentum Pi = mvi and final momentum Pf = mvf, wrote ΔP = m(vf - vi), and divided by time t to prove F = ΔP/t.

questions.questionText: Sara has a mass of 30 kg. While running in the playground, she accelerates from 2 m/s to 4 m/s in 5 s. Calculate the power consumed in the given situation.
questions.sloText: Solve word problems on the concept of power.
checkingHints: 1 mark for listing given data (m = 30 kg, vi = 2 m/s, vf = 4 m/s, t = 5 s)
1 mark for calculating acceleration a = (4 - 2)/5 = 0.4 m/s²
1 mark for calculating force F = ma = 30 × 0.4 = 12 N
1 mark for calculating distance S = vit + ½at² = 15 m (or work via ΔKE = ½m(vf² - vi²) = 180 J)
1 mark for calculating work W = F × S = 180 J
1 mark for calculating power P = W/t = 180/5 = 36 W
questions.overallPerformance: Most candidates attempted this part and showed varied ability to chain kinematics, force/work, and power equations.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses systematically calculated acceleration (0.4 m/s²), force (12 N), distance (15 m), work (180 J), and power (36 W) with proper SI units.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses combined numbers arbitrarily without applying F = ma or P = W/t and omitted units.
suggestions: Teach multi-step problem decomposition: Given Data → Acceleration → Force & Distance (or ΔKE) → Work → Power (P = W/t).
questions.modelAnswer: Better responses systematically calculated acceleration (0.4 m/s²), force (12 N), distance (15 m), work (180 J), and power (36 W) with proper SI units.

questions.questionText:
i. Explain why the walls of a dam filled with water are usually wedge-shaped. Relate this to the pressure of liquid at different depths.
ii. If the density of water is 1,000 kg/m³, then calculate the depth of water in a dam when the pressure at the bottom is 1,00,000 Pa. (Note: Take the value of acceleration due to gravity as 9.8 m/s².)
questions.sloText: Solve word problems on the concept of pressure beneath a liquid to depth and to density.
checkingHints: Part i: 1 mark for each reason relating depth, hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh, and thicker base wall strength (3 marks)
Part ii: 1 mark for formula P = ρgh, 1 mark for substitution 100,000 = 1000 × 9.8 × h, 1 mark for answer h = 10.2 m (3 marks)
questions.overallPerformance: Candidates who understood hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh connected dam thickness at the base to greater water pressure at depth and solved accurately for h = 10.2 m.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses explained that liquid pressure increases directly with depth (P = ρgh), requiring a wider, stronger base to withstand higher lateral forces, and calculated h = 100,000 / (1000 × 9.8) = 10.2 m.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses gave non-scientific explanations (e.g., preventing tsunamis) and divided numbers arbitrarily without using P = ρgh.
suggestions: Use pressure-depth diagrams showing water jets emerging from different heights of a cylinder to visualise P = ρgh and why dam walls widen toward the base.
questions.modelAnswer: Better responses explained that liquid pressure increases directly with depth (P = ρgh), requiring a wider, stronger base to withstand higher lateral forces, and calculated h = 100,000 / (1000 × 9.8) = 10.2 m.

pedagogies.name: Storyboard
pedagogies.description: A visual pedagogy that uses a series of illustrated panels to present a narrative, helping learners organise ideas, sequence events, and comprehend complex concepts.

pedagogies.name: Cause and Effect
pedagogies.description: Explores relationships between actions and physical consequences so learners understand how variables and physical events are interconnected.

pedagogies.name: Fish and Bone
pedagogies.description: Breaks down complex topics into main ideas (the fish) and supporting details (the bones) to highlight essential concepts and explanations.

pedagogies.name: Concept Mapping
pedagogies.description: Visually represents relationships between physical quantities and laws by connecting key concepts into a structured network.

pedagogies.name: Audio Visual Resources
pedagogies.description: Incorporates animations, simulations, and video demonstrations to make abstract physical phenomena observable and engaging.

pedagogies.name: Think, Pair, and Share
pedagogies.description: Collaborative technique where students reason through a problem individually, compare with a partner, and share with the class.

pedagogies.name: Questioning Technique (Socratic Approach)
pedagogies.description: Stimulates critical thinking by posing probing questions that require students to justify physical reasoning and assumptions.

pedagogies.name: Practical Demonstration
pedagogies.description: Hands-on laboratory or classroom demonstrations that bridge theoretical equations with real-world physical measurements.
